newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori tells rebels to give up fight.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori tells rebels to give up fight.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori told Marxist rebels holding about 340 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home for a fifth day on Sunday he would not use force against them if they surrendered their arms and freed all captives.
In a blunt speech broadcast on local television and radio late on Saturday night, Fujimori said:
"The proposal is concrete: that the captors surrender their weapons to a guarantor committee and that they allow the evacuation of all the hostages without exception.
"In this way the possibility of force being used by the Peruvian state will be ruled out and from there, with all guarantees, a way out can be studied."
The president's uncompromising stance received swift approval from Japan, which, after Peru, has the largest number of hostages in the compound.

"The proposal as a whole is the appropriate solution to a peaceful resolution to the crisis and the preservation of the lives of the hostages," said Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who was in Lima to help negotiate. His comments were quickly echoed in Tokyo by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto
Japan's support appeared to smoothe over differences between Lima and Tokyo, which had previously said the two government's were "far apart" in their ideas over the crisis.

Fujimori's speech, delivered in a rapid, stern voice, was his first public statement since about 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the residence on Tuesday in a carefully-planned commando assault.
Witnesses outside the ambassador's residence reported a slight build-up of security forces shortly after Fujimori's address.

But there was no immediate response from rebels inside the elegant building, which was thrown into total darkness shortly before the speech when a power generator ran out of fuel. Early in the crisis, Fujimori ordered electricity, water and telephone lines to the residence cut.

The rebel group's leader, Nestor Cerpa, had earlier promised gradually to free all hostages not linked to the government. Rebels have released over 100 hostages since the start of the crisis. All of the remaining captives were men.

After speaking via walkie-talkie to Peru's America Television, Cerpa -- one of the country's two most wanted men -- passed the radio to Peru's hostage Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki.

The two men said they were being treated well and that rebels were ready to negotiate a peaceful end to the saga. Like hostages already released, Tuleda and Aoki warned efforts to free them by force would cost many lives.
After a second meeting with Fujimori late on Saturday, Ikeda said the Peruvian leader seemed weathered but more confident than during their first encounter on Thursday.
"Although there is no change in his resolve to break the stalemate, I felt that in the earlier meeting, he seemed undecided about what exactly to do.
"But tonight, although he looked weary from concentration, I felt a sense of confidence from him that a way out will definitely open up," he added.

Police confirmed Cerpa as the leader of the heavily armed rebels who seized the residence and took prisoner a glittering array of high-ranking hostages including foreign ambassadors, two ministers and Peru's anti-terrorism chief.

Fujimori has maintained a tough stance in the saga, refusing to bow to repeated pleas from hostages to reconnect power and other services to the building. He told local newspaper editors on Friday he had no plans even to talk to the rebels.
Well-known for his strongarm tactics, Fujimori refused to give in to the MRTA's demands that he free more than 400 of their jailed comrades.

"They hope for dialogue by placing an AKM rifle to the neck of hostages. My government is not prepared to accept that the force and violence of a terrorist command can be imposed on 23 million people, who reject these methods, which are neither civilised or political," he said in his address.
Fujimori, whose previous successes against Peru's guerrillas helped him to a landslide reelection victory in 1995, won immediate backing for his speech.

"This is a strong position, just as it should be, because you cannot be weak," said nightwatchman Julio Policarpo outside a Lima bank. "However, it also allows a dialogue. Without talks they (the rebels) could produce a more drastic situation and sacrifice hostages."

Inside the residence, victims spent their fifth night sleeping on the floor in crumpled and smelly suits, suffering from stinking overcrowded toilets, poor food, stifling heat and overcrowding, Red Cross officials said.

The Red Cross continued efforts to relieve the hostages' plight on Saturday with deliveries of meals and fresh clothes. But efforts to take in flashlights overnight were denied by police surrounding the residence.
A Peruvian television station showed the first still images, sent in anonymously, of hostages inside the building.

The Panamericana Television photographs showed several men, still dressed in elegant shirts and pants, living in cramped conditions. In most cases they looked relaxed and many were smiling. No MRTA rebels were shown in the photographs.

Several thousand Peruvians packed Lima's central square, the Plaza de Armas, late on Saturday to celebrate an emotional outdoor mass for the hostages. Peru's leading ecclesiastics led the service as people sang, prayed and held candles.
Some shouted "Long live liberty!" "Long live Peru!"
In Washington, Defence Secretary William Perry declined comment on Saturday when asked about unspecified reports that elite U.S. Delta Force commandos were ready to move to help rescue the hostages.
"I will not comment on any action that is planned or not planned relative to dealing with that. Simply because lives of people are at stake," Perry said in a videotaped interview on CNN.
